title: NPV vs PV: which discounting function do you need?
meta_desc: NPV vs PV in spreadsheets: constant payments vs varying cash flows, the off-by-one timing trap in NPV, and when XNPV is the honest answer.
intro: Both discount future money to today. PV handles the special case of IDENTICAL payments at regular intervals (annuities, loans); NPV takes a list of DIFFERENT cash flows. The trap everyone hits: NPV discounts its very first argument by one full period — it assumes your first flow happens a period from now, not today.

cols: One constant payment (plus optional lump sum)
A list, each with its own DATE
First flow = END of period 1 (discounted once!)
It's the result — PV is the willing-to-pay-today number

when.use_when: Valuing streams of equal payments: what a loan, lease, annuity, or bond coupon leg is worth today.
Project appraisal with varying yearly flows — remembering the initial investment is added OUTSIDE the function, undiscounted.
Real-world dated cash flows (deals close mid-month, payments cluster) — the assumptions disappear because every flow carries its date.

compat_note: All three execute identically in every LibreOffice version we test (desktop Excel behavior per docs — we do not run desktop Excel; Google Sheets is executed separately, see each function page) — including the NPV first-flow discounting convention (verified: NPV(10%,100,200,300)=481.59, where 100 is divided by 1.1 once) and XNPV returning 0 when discounting at the flows' own IRR. Excel for the web is a separate application with its own calculation engine, and that one we do execute: all 3 corpus cases for these functions matched the documented values there (recalculated on OneDrive, 2026-09-01); the per-case values are on the individual function pages.
